displayQuote: Can't somebody bring me a one-handed economist?

meta.title: Who really said "Can't somebody bring me a one-handed economist?"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No contemporary record ties this line to Truman. The exact wording first surfaces in 1974, second-hand, in Edwin Nourse's New York Times obituary.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Can't somebody bring me a one-handed economist?'?
meta.ogDescription: Truman gets the credit everywhere, but the joke is older than his presidency and the wording is only documented from 1974. Here is what the record shows.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Credited to Truman almost everywhere the line appears, but nothing contemporary ties it to him. The exact wording is first documented in 1974, second-hand, when the economist Walter W. Heller told a meeting of the American Economic Association that Truman had shouted it after listening to his economic adviser Edwin Nourse — a scene that, if it happened, happened in 1949 or earlier.

source.heading: Where the wording actually appears

docMeta.dd: Edwin Nourse, 90, Dies; Truman’s Economic Aide, Sought Anonymity
The New York Times, 10 April 1974, by Steven R. Weisman
Walter W. Heller, at a meeting of the American Economic Association — a second-hand account
1949 or earlier, if genuine: Edwin Nourse chaired the Council of Economic Advisers 1946–1949

source.excerpt: At a meeting of the American Economic Association, Walter W. Heller [...] said that Dr. Nourse was a classic “on the one hand—on the other hand” economist and that he infuriated President Truman with his failure to present a clear policy for him to adopt. Finally, Dr. Heller said, Mr. Truman shouted: “Can’t somebody bring me a one-handed economist?”
trail: 1936 — the earliest known ancestor of the joke: a Scripps-Howard editorial complains that what the Republicans need is a “one-armed platform writer,” years before Truman reached the White House ↗.

1951–1963 — the gag circulates freely, told about a tax consultant’s client, an Alabama judge, Defense Secretary Charles E. Wilson, a Colorado attorney general and a New York banker, with no mention of Truman in the 1960s citations ↗.

10 April 1974 — three days after Nourse’s death, The New York Times obituary carries Walter Heller’s account of Truman shouting for a one-handed economist: the first time the line is attached to Truman in print ↗.

1986, reported 2019 — a Truman Library archivist says that to the best of his knowledge the library holds no recording of the remark, but relays a 1986 telephone conversation in which John R. Steelman recalled Truman asking him, “John, do you think you could find me a one-armed economist?” — indirect corroboration, four decades on ↗.
source.excerptNote: As printed in Edwin Nourse’s obituary in The New York Times, 10 April 1974 — the earliest attribution to Truman that Quote Investigator has found, and a recollection of a remark said to date from 1949 or earlier.

source.rightsNote: No work written or published by Truman contains this sentence; it survives only as a remark other people remembered. The earliest text that carries the wording is a 1974 New York Times obituary, which is itself in copyright, so nothing here can be called public domain — the seven-word quip has no identifiable published origin to assign a status to.

author.name: Harry S. Truman
author.kicker: The man it is pinned to
author.heading: About Harry S. Truman
author.bio: Harry S. Truman was born in Missouri on 8 May 1884 and became the 33rd President of the United States, serving from 1945 until 1953. In 1946 he appointed the Brookings economist Edwin G. Nourse to head the newly created Council of Economic Advisers, a post Nourse held until 1949 — the working relationship at the centre of this anecdote. Truman died on 26 December 1972; no recording or contemporary document of the “one-handed economist” remark has ever been produced.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented in Steven R. Weisman, “Edwin Nourse, 90, Dies; Truman’s Economic Aide, Sought Anonymity,” The New York Times, 10 April 1974, p. 44 — quoted and dated in Quote Investigator, “Quote Origin: Can’t Somebody Bring Me a One-Handed Economist?” 10 April 2019. No contemporary source for the remark is known.

copyAttribution: "Can't somebody bring me a one-handed economist?" — attributed to Harry S. Truman (1884–1972). No contemporary source. The wording is first documented second-hand in Edwin Nourse's New York Times obituary, 10 April 1974; the joke itself was circulating about other professions by 1936. Via Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Everyone’s favourite economist joke, and its uncertain owner
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabricated quote so much as an orphaned one. The joke was in circulation before Truman reached the White House, was told about several different professions, and only attached itself to him in print long after he left office — which is why sites that print it with a confident date are printing something nobody can show you.

items.why: Repeated everywhere, sourced almost nowhere — the Foundation for Economic Education, for instance, tells the story with no citation or date at all ↗. Barry Popik’s survey of the printed record concludes that there is no evidence associating the joke with Truman’s administration ↗.

In January 1956 a Washington newspaper item ran the same gag about the Defense Secretary, reporting that Wilson could use a “good one-handed man” because subordinates kept saying on the one hand this and the other hand that — years before Truman’s name was ever attached to it in print ↗.

items.who: A tax consultant, an Alabama judge, a Colorado attorney general, anonymous businessmen
items.why: Quote Investigator tracks the quip through a 1951 “one-armed tax man,” a 1955 “one-armed man for president” of the state bar, a 1957 “one-armed lawyer” and a 1960 “one handed attorney general” — a template that could be fitted to any hedging profession ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest published instance of the joke that Quote Investigator has located is a 1936 Scripps-Howard editorial calling for a “one-armed platform writer” — and the earliest version pinned to Truman is a second-hand anecdote printed in 1974 ↗. He may well have said it; the paper trail simply starts long after he could confirm it.

context.heading: Why a president wanted an economist with one arm
lead: The gag needs no explanation to anyone who has ever asked an expert a yes-or-no question. An adviser lays out the case “on the one hand,” then turns it over “on the other hand,” and the person who has to actually decide something is left holding two answers and no decision. Amputate a limb, the joke runs, and you get a straight reply.

Truman had a natural foil for it. Edwin G. Nourse, the Brookings economist he appointed in 1946 to chair the brand-new Council of Economic Advisers, was in the job until 1949 ↗ and had a scholar’s reluctance to hand a politician a single recommendation. Both surviving accounts of the remark put Nourse in the room. What neither account is, is contemporary: the first was published in 1974 and the second was a telephone recollection given in 1986, and Quote Investigator notes that both came decades after the events they describe ↗.
context.detailsSummary: The competing wordings, and where each one actually comes from
detailsBody: “Can’t somebody bring me a one-handed economist?” — Walter W. Heller’s account, as printed in Edwin Nourse’s New York Times obituary of 10 April 1974. This is the earliest attribution to Truman that Quote Investigator has found ↗.

“John, do you think you could find me a one-armed economist?” — what John R. Steelman, Truman’s Assistant to the President, recalled in a 1986 telephone conversation with Truman Library staff, as relayed by archivist Randy Sowell in 2019 ↗. Same scene, different limb.

“Get me a one-handed economist! All my economists say, ‘on the one hand, . . . but on the other.’” — as printed in Paul F. Boller’s Presidential Anecdotes (1996), where the supporting citation is an indirect one from 1980 ↗.

“Give me a one-handed economist!” — the form that actually circulates on the quote aggregators, where Goodreads, AZQuotes and Quotefancy all print it as a flat Truman quotation with no citation of any kind. It is Boller’s sentence with the verb changed, one step further from a source that was already indirect.
context.pull: The joke is older than the president it belongs to.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator finds no solidly-dated contemporary evidence that Truman used the joke; the earliest published attribution to him is the 10 April 1974 New York Times obituary of Edwin Nourse (by Steven R. Weisman, p. 44), in which Walter W. Heller, at an American Economic Association meeting, recounted that Truman shouted 'Can't somebody bring me a one-handed economist?'. The earliest known instance of the joke family is a 1936 Scripps-Howard editorial about a 'one-armed platform writer'; later versions involve a 1951 tax man, a 1955 judge, Charles E. Wilson in a January 1956 Washington Post and Times Herald item, a 1957 lawyer, a 1960 Colorado attorney general and a 1963 New York banker. In 2019 Truman Library archivist Randy Sowell said the library has no recording, and relayed a 1986 telephone account from John R. Steelman quoting Truman as saying 'John, do you think you could find me a one-armed economist?'. Nourse resigned in 1949, so the scene would predate that; QI notes uncertainty remains because both accounts came decades later. Boller's Presidential Anecdotes (1996) carries the 'Get me a one-handed economist!' form supported by an indirect 1980 citation; Keyes (1995) uses an indirect 1985 citation.

Barry Popik's entry (dated 30 December 2010) states there is no evidence associating the joke with Truman's administration (1945-1953), gives Truman's dates as 1884-1972, says none of the 1960s citations mentions Truman, and shows a 1966 source crediting Charles E. Wilson of General Motors; it also quotes Murray Weidenbaum (2005) calling it Truman's 'famous if not mythical' call for a one-armed economist.

The Truman Library finding aid states Edwin Griswold Nourse was born 20 May 1883, was appointed by Truman in 1946 to head the new Council of Economic Advisers, held the post until 1949, and died on 7 April 1974.

Wikipedia gives Harry S. Truman's birth date as 8 May 1884 and death as 26 December 1972, and describes him as the 33rd president of the United States, serving 1945-1953; the article does not mention any 'one-handed' or 'one-armed economist' remark.

Wikipedia's article on Edwin Griswold Nourse (1883-1974) identifies him as the first Chair of the Council of Economic Advisers and does not mention or quote any Truman remark about a one-handed or one-armed economist.
Wikiquote's Harry S. Truman page contains no version of the 'one-handed economist' or 'one-armed economist' quip in any section, including Sourced, Attributed, Disputed and Misattributed.

NPR's The Indicator from Planet Money, episode 'An Indicator In The Hand' (29 March 2019), opens with the host stating that President Harry Truman once sarcastically asked a member of his staff if he could find him a one-armed economist, with no source cited in the transcript.

AZQuotes (quote ID 604127) prints "Give me a one-handed economist! All my economists say, On the one hand on the other." as a flat Harry S. Truman quotation with no source, book, date or citation of any kind; Goodreads (quote 7887683) and Quotefancy (quote 1448691) carry the same 'Give me' wording. Quote Investigator's page contains no 'Give me' string: the form it documents from Paul F. Boller's Presidential Anecdotes (1996) reads "Get me a one-handed economist!"
The FEE article repeats the Truman attribution ('Give me a one-armed economist, he demanded') without citing any source or date for the anecdote.
